01 — Overview
Project Abstract

This project implements and controls a BLDC motor controller capable of efficient, precise motor operation. The system uses 6-step commutation for fundamental control, and Adaptive Tabu Search (ATS) for automatic PID gain tuning.

Practical focus areas include direction control via commutation-sequence reversal, PID-based closed-loop speed regulation, and ADC-driven duty cycle adjustment through a potentiometer. Speed feedback is derived from the Hall sensor output frequency, giving real-time rotor speed for the closed-loop controller.

The result is a reliable, bidirectional, and efficient BLDC drive with improved speed stability and smooth commutation, verified on a modular XPO-PEDEB bench trainer.

02 — Architecture
System Overview
01
⚡

DSP Controller (XPO-EST)

Texas Instruments TMS320F28335 running at 100 MHz generates PWM gate signals, reads Hall sensor feedback, and executes 6-step commutation, FOC, and SVPWM algorithms.

02
🔌

IGBT Power Panels (PE7/L & PE7/R)

Eight 1200 V / 40 A IGBT modules arranged as a three-phase inverter bridge. Each module has an integrated isolated gate driver and overcurrent/overtemperature protection.

03
🔄

BLDC Motor + DC Generator

3-phase PM brushless DC motor (160 V, 3000 RPM) mechanically coupled to a separately excited DC generator for dynamic load testing and performance characterisation.

04
📡

Hall Sensor Feedback

Three Hall-effect sensors provide rotor position for commutation sequencing. Speed is derived from Hall signal frequency, enabling accurate closed-loop PID speed control.

05
📊

Supply & Measurement Panels

EMT8 (±12 V / +5 V supply), EMT23 (variable AC/DC via dimmer), EMT6B (DC voltmeter/ammeter 0–300 V, 0–5 A), and EMT34 (AC measurements via CTs).

06
🎛️

User Interface & Load

Push buttons and potentiometers for manual speed/direction control. Lamp load panel (EMT7) with 100 W & 200 W bulbs in star configuration for generator loading.

04 — Control
Control Algorithm
1

Hall Sensor Position Detection

Three Hall sensors generate a 3-bit code. Each unique code maps to one of six 60° electrical sectors, determining which two motor phases to energise.

2

6-Step Commutation Logic

Two phases active at a time (120° trapezoidal). The DSP decodes Hall signals, selects the commutation state, and drives the corresponding IGBT gate signals with 7.64 µs dead time.

3

PWM Duty Cycle Modulation

Speed is varied by adjusting the PWM duty cycle via push-button switches or an ADC potentiometer, directly controlling the average voltage applied to the motor.

4

PID Closed-Loop Speed Control

The PID controller compares actual rotor speed (from Hall signal frequency) to the reference setpoint and adjusts PWM duty cycle to minimise error.

5

Adaptive Tabu Search (ATS) Tuning

ATS auto-tunes Kp, Ki, Kd by minimising a sum-of-squared-errors objective function — outperforming Ziegler–Nichols with faster rise time and lower overshoot.

6

Direction Reversal

Reversing the commutation sequence (CW → CCW) is achieved by a single switch, instantly swapping the phase energisation order for seamless bidirectional operation.

07 — Conclusion
Discussion & Future Scope

The implementation of the BLDC motor drive using 6-step commutation combined with Adaptive Tabu Search PID optimisation proved to be an effective approach for precise, bidirectional speed and direction control.

Hardware experiments confirmed real-world applicability via PWM duty cycle modulation at 150 V DC, yielding 824 RPM at ~90% duty cycle. MATLAB simulation corroborated commutation sequences and motor response. ATS integration improved system responsiveness by adaptively optimising Kp, Ki, and Kd without manual intervention — outperforming classical Ziegler–Nichols tuning on settling time, rise time, and overshoot.

A key challenge was that the SIMULINK model required a Texas Instruments license to generate F28335-compatible embedded C code from Simulink — highlighting a practical gap between simulation and direct hardware deployment.

Future Scope

  • Implement Field Oriented Control (FOC) on the existing bench to achieve smoother torque control and lower torque ripple compared to 6-step commutation.
  • Deploy sensorless back-EMF detection to eliminate Hall sensors, improving reliability and reducing component count for EV applications.
  • Port ATS-tuned PID code directly to the TMS320F28335 using TI's embedded C toolchain once proper licensing is acquired.
  • Extend the platform to test electric vehicle propulsion drives, integrating regenerative braking and torque-speed curve characterisation.
  • Explore advanced AI/ML-based controllers (reinforcement learning, neural network PID) for adaptive performance under varying load conditions.
